Thank you for your patience. ::: :::: ## Comprehension questions The questions below come from the [Deployments and Code Promotion](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-5-deployments.html) chapter. ### Data Science Environments > ***Write down a mental map of the relationship between the three environments for data science. Include the following terms: Git Promote, CI/CD, automation, deployment, dev, test, prod.*** The three environments for data science are: development, test, and production (not to be confused with the three *layers* of data science environments[^layers]). The figures from the [chapter](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-5-deployments.html#separate-the-prod-environment) do an excellent job illustrating these environments, but I've added a mindmap: [^layers]: These [three layers](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-1-env-as-code.html#environments-have-layers) are Packages (Python + R Packages), System (Python + R Packages, Other System Libraries, and Operating System), and Hardware (Virtual Hardware and Physical Hardware). ```{=html} ``` ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Data Science Environments' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: center %%{init: {'look': 'handDrawn', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"18px"}}}%% mindmap root((Code
Promotion)) Dev Code Writing Experimentation Git Promote Push to feature branch Pull request triggers CI/CD Test Automation Unit tests Integration tests UAT CI/CD Validates build Runs test suite Prod Deployment Automated release Version tagged Monitoring Stability checks Access control ``` #### DEV Environments The development environment (**dev**) is the primary location where data scientists write new code. It's typically used for iteration and experimentation, and it's connected to version control (Git). #### Test Environments The testing environment (**test**) is a mirror of the production environment with realistic data (often anonymized). Test environments are integrated and validates with other systems, and user acceptance testing occurs here. #### Production Environments The 'live' environment that serves the end users is the production environment (**prod**). Prod has strictly controlled access with a focus on stability and monitoring. ### Git & Data Science > ***Why is Git so important to a good code promotion strategy?*** Code promotion is the process of tagging a Git commit as ready for production. This creates a reference point, and if desired, can trigger a production deployment pipeline. If a change isn’t represented as a Git commit, it literally didn’t happen. Code promotion ensures consistency across all three environments and reduces human error in deployment. All commits are signed--we know who made the changes--and the prod branch requires approval to merge (i.e., it's protected). This artifact immutability connects 'builds' to specific commit SHAs or by tagging releases. The same code is promoted across environments so we can be sure untested code never reaches production. Without Git, the code would need to be rebuilt in each environment, and the tested code wouldn't necessarily be the deployed code, causing environment drift. Environment drift is when the code in production differs from the code that was tested. In DevOps, environment drift is the enemy because it leads to unpredictable behavior and makes debugging difficult. Git enables environment parity. The three environments (dev, test, and prod) differ only by data and credentials, and changes are promoted, not re-created. When production inevitably breaks, we can use Git to roll back by redeploying previous commits/tags. This avoids making ad-hoc changes in a production server. ----------------------------------------------------------- > ***Can you have a code promotion strategy without Git?*** Sure — code promotion can be done without Git, but you'd need to find a way to: * Create some kind of 'immutable versioned artifact' (i.e., something to be promoted) * Blocks/gates requiring tests/approvals that must be passed before promotion * A promotion mechanism to copy/move/retag the immutable versioned artifact between environments Also need substitutes for: 1. A way to view/review 'diffs', either by performing code review (or document-style review) on release bundles 2. The ability to keep previous artifacts and switch the environments 3. Some means of traceability that connects the artifacts, manifests, approvals, and build logs ### Git & CI/CD > ***What is the relationship between Git and CI/CD?*** A CI/CD Pipeline is an automated process that builds, tests, and deploys the code. In CI-CD systems, Git defines the code promotion workflow, but not the pipeline. The pipeline simply *reacts* to Git events. The code promotion logic lives in the Git branches, tags, merge policies, but not in brittle pipeline scripts. This enables a "build once, promote many times" strategy, where the same tested artifact is promoted across environments. Git provides the code change/approval history, and the pipeline results tied to commits. Each release is also tagged, making it easy to track commits and introduced changes. This traceability is crucial for debugging and accountability. Git serves as the gatekeeper for CI-CD policies and integrates directly with enforcement mechanisms. Using Git turns CI-CD into a system, not a script. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Git & CI/CD' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: center %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'look': 'handDrawn', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"18px"}}}%% flowchart LR GitEv["Git Event
(push, PR, merge)"] -->|"triggers"| CICD["CI/CD Pipeline"] CICD --> CI["Continuous
Integration (CI)
Build & Test"] CICD --> CD["Continuous
Delivery (CD)
Deploy"] style GitEv fill:#F9E79F,stroke:#D4AC0D,color:#000 style CICD fill:#D4E6F1,stroke:#2E86C1,color:#000 style CI fill:#D5F5E3,stroke:#1E8449,color:#000 style CD fill:#FADBD8,stroke:#C0392B,color:#000 ``` Think of Git as the source of truth and CI/CD as an automated response to changes in that truth. Git events — pushes, pull requests, merges — can fire a CI/CD pipeline. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Git & CI/CD' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: center %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'look': 'handDrawn', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"18px"}}}%% sequenceDiagram actor Dev as Developer participant Git as Git participant CI as CI Pipeline participant CD as CD Pipeline participant Test as Test Env participant Prod as Prod Env Dev->>Git: Push to feature branch Git->>CI: Triggers build & tests CI-->>Dev: ✅ Tests pass / ❌ Fail Dev->>Git: Merge PR to main Git->>CD: Triggers deployment CD->>Test: Deploy to test env CD-->>Dev: ✅ Test deployment confirmed Dev->>Git: Tag release (v1.0) Git->>CD: Triggers production deployment CD->>Prod: Deploy to prod env ``` **Key distinctions between Git and CI/CD:** | | Git | CI/CD | |---|---|---| | **Role** | Tracks & versions code | Automates build, test, deploy | | **Trigger** | Human action (commit, merge) | Git events | | **Output** | A versioned history | A tested, deployed artifact | ----------------------------------------------------------- > ***What’s the benefit of using Git and CI/CD together?*** Without Git, CI/CD has no reliable source to build from. Without CI/CD, Git changes require manual promotion between environments — which is slow and error-prone. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Git & CI/CD' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: center %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'look': 'handDrawn', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"18px"}}}%% gitGraph commit id: "Initial commit" branch feature checkout feature commit id: "New feature code" commit id: "Unit tests pass ✅" checkout main merge feature id: "Merge PR → triggers CI" commit id: "Deploy to Test ✅" commit id: "UAT approved ✅" commit id: "Tag release v1.0 → triggers CD" branch prod checkout prod commit id: "Deploy to Prod 🚀" ``` In the `gitGraph` above: 1. The `feature` branch is where the developer writes and tests code locally 2. When a pull request is merged to `main`, this fires the CI pipeline (build & test) and deploys to `test` 3. `v1.0` is tagged to a release on the `main` branch, which fires the CD pipeline and deploys to `prod` 4. The `prod` branch represents the exact code running in the live environment, providing a clear snapshot for auditing and rollback ### Git, GitHub, CI/CD, Actions, & Version Control > ***Write out a mental map of the relationship of the following terms: Git, GitHub, CI/CD, GitHub Actions, Version Control.*** ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Git, GitHub, CI/CD, Actions, & Version Control' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: center %%{init: {'look': 'handDrawn', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"18px"}}}%% mindmap root((Code
Management)) Version Control Tracks changes over time Enables rollback Supports collaboration Git Local repositories Branching and merging Commit history GitHub Remote repositories Pull requests Code review GitHubActions Workflow files Triggered by Git events CICD Continuous Integration Automated testing Build validation Continuous Delivery Automated deployment Environment promotion ```
